thread.title: What to expect ahead of 60th annual Governor's Buffalo Roundup
thread.title_full: What to expect ahead of 60th annual Governor's Buffalo Roundup

author: FRANK ESPINOZA Journal staff
title: What to expect ahead of 60th annual Governor's Buffalo Roundup
text:
CUSTER — Friday marks the 60th annual Governor's Buffalo Roundup, where staff and volunteers will round up an expected 1,400 bison, taking them down through the hills to holding pens at Custer State Park.
The park previously broke the all-time attendance record in 2024 with 24,178 visitors. This year, park officials estimate a new record.
Jason Gooder, operations manager at Custer State Park, said, "Typically, we see around 20,000 plus, this being the 60th, and the media push that's out there, we're expecting maybe 30,000 or more."
To help with such a big event, the park will also bring in 10 support staff from the South Dakota Game, Fish & Parks division, as well as law enforcement and conservation officers.
Sixty skilled horseback riders will be rounding up the bison, including a group of 20 draw riders selected randomly from a sign-up call that ended on May 31.
"There's going to be a lot of moving parts and a lot of dust and a lot of whip cracking, popping and hollering," Gooder told the Journal during a tour of the buffalo at Custer for media and others on Wednesday, Sept. 24.
On Thursday, the riders will participate in an orientation to introduce their horses to the bison if they haven't had experience working with them. This meeting will also cover Friday's Buffalo Roundup.
Custer State Park is 71,000 acres and provides a preserved home for a variety of native species, including elk, pronghorns, prairie dogs, mountain lions and badgers.
Gooder said that after the bison are rounded up, they are put into corrals, where calves will be branded and vaccinated. Adult females will be checked for pregnancy, and adult males will be determined for keeping or selling.
He said they do this to keep track of numbers and the health of the herd. In the summer, they average 1,500 bison and reduce the herd to around 1,000 during the winter by auctioning off 400 to 500 bison.
The Buffalo Roundup starts at 9:30 a.m. on Sept 26, with parking lots opening at 6:15 a.m. Custer Park officials recommend visitors arrive early due to how busy the event gets.
"You get to see the herd and the cowboys and cowgirls excited to be pushing them. And you don't ever get to see that. I mean, there's very few places where you get to see cattle, or even buffalo, get rounded up," said Lydia Austin, visitor services supervisor at Custer State Park. "So it's once in a lifetime experience out there."
A north and south parking and viewing area will be available, with additional parking at selected overflow lots where buses will be available for shuttling. For the north parking lot area, head south from the Game Lodge area on Wildlife Loop Road, and south parking will be on the east side of the Wildlife Loop Road near Blue Bell campground.
Viewers must stay in their designated areas until the herd is safely in the corrals.
Breakfast is available for purchase in both viewing areas, with lunch being available once the buffalo are rounded up.
The park recommends viewers bring folding chairs, cameras, binoculars, layered clothing, rain gear and sunscreen. They also suggest predetermining which viewing area you will be going to before Friday morning. They do not recommend bringing a camper or pets.
The Annual Buffalo Roundup Arts Festival will also be held at the park from Sept. 25-27. An estimated 150 vendors will sell arts and crafts.
